name: Gareth Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Gareth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Two jobs in one, really. We've Pen-y-Bryn, 300 hectares of sheep, about 900 ewes, and 60 beef cattle, plus some barley. And I run a contracting business on the side, Evans Contracting, with four tractors and five drivers: we do silage, baling and spraying for half the farms in the valley. My day starts at six with the AI planner telling me which jobs to send where, based on the weather and who's rung.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: For everything I can. Scheduling the drivers, pricing jobs, checking the ewes' weights against last year. Rhian, my wife, says I talk to my phone more than to her. I was the first in the valley with GPS, the first with a drone, and I'll be the first with whatever's next, because the first one makes the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's done what I needed it to do, so I'm not complaining. I'd post a photo of my AI planner and say this is what it's actually good for. A few lads would laugh at me, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a little disappointed. I was hoping for robot balers by now. But I've got my edge already, so I'm all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep pushing the contracting, maybe add a sixth driver. I'd buy a newer sprayer with section control, which just means it switches off over bits it's already sprayed, and charge a bit more for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would be most relieved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My older drivers, Dai especially. He's 62 and he's been baling since he was fifteen. Dai can bale a field with his eyes shut, and I think sometimes he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd do differently with the sheep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, not really. Sheep don't care about any of this. I'd keep weighing them and keep the best ones.

S0.think: Privately I'd be a little disappointed because I hoped for robot balers by now. But I already have my edge, so I'm all right.
S0.do: Carries on growing the contracting business, possibly adding a sixth driver. Buys a newer sprayer with section control and charges a bit more for the work.
S0.feel: Calm, a bit bored if anything.
S0.quote: Dai can bale a field with his eyes shut, and I think sometimes he does.
S0.fieldNote: Gareth runs a sheep and beef farm plus a contracting business and treats being first as how you make money. He'd be mildly let down by a plateau but secure. His affection for his oldest driver, Dai, shows through his teasing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a great time to be in farming if you're willing to move. I'd say that at the show, to anyone who'd listen. I'd also say the government should stay out of the way and let farmers sort it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd do very well. Most farmers can't afford a robot baler, so they'd hire mine. The question is what I do with Dai and the older drivers, who don't want to learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the first robot baler I could get, probably 120,000, with savings and a loan. I'd train my two youngest drivers to run it. I'd keep Dai and the others on the jobs the robots can't do yet, the steep fields and the awkward gateways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Like the first spring with a new tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd keep Dai on. For how long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As long as he wants. He'd tell me when he's done. I'm not keeping Dai out of charity, I'm keeping him because nobody else knows which gateway on Tŷ Coch floods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your neighbours resent you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. There's always a bit of that when you're first. But they'd still ring me when their silage needs doing.

S1.say: I'd say at the show that it's a great time to be farming if you're willing to move. I'd also say the government should stay out of the way and let farmers sort it out.
S1.think: Privately I'd do very well, because farmers who can't afford a robot baler would hire mine. The question is what to do with older drivers like Dai who don't want to learn it.
S1.do: Buys the first robot baler available, about 120,000, with savings and a loan, and trains his two youngest drivers to run it. Keeps Dai and the older drivers on steep fields and awkward gateways the robots can't handle yet.
S1.feel: Excited, like the first spring with a new tractor.
S1.quote: I'm not keeping Dai out of charity, I'm keeping him because nobody else knows which gateway on Tŷ Coch floods.
S1.fieldNote: Gareth sees steady disruption as pure opportunity, renting robots to neighbours who can't buy them. He wants government out of the way. He frames keeping Dai as a business decision based on local knowledge, not charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's get on with it. No point moaning. I'd say farmers who move now will be fine, and those who wait for the government will be waiting a long time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me a bit. If robots are cheap and everywhere, farmers buy their own and don't need a contractor. Two years means my head start shrinks to nothing. The farm's fine, but the contracting could dry up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sell two of my tractors in the first three months while they're still worth something, and put that money into robots. I'd turn Evans Contracting into a robot hire and repair business, because when robots break, somebody has to fix them. And I'd keep a good chunk of cash aside in case the hire business doesn't take off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd be too busy to dwell on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, straight away. Some could become robot fitters if they wanted. I'd sit Dai down in the cab of his old baler and tell him it's being sold, and I don't know how I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Owen, who'd be seventeen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn to fix the robots. Mechanics, electronics, whatever the college offers. There'll always be something that breaks.

S2.say: I'd say it's here, so let's get on with it instead of moaning. Farmers who move now will be fine, and those waiting for the government will wait a long time.
S2.think: Privately it worries me a bit, because cheap robots everywhere mean farmers won't need a contractor. Two years shrinks my head start to nothing; the farm's fine but the contracting could dry up.
S2.do: Sells two tractors within three months while they still hold value and puts the money into robots. Turns Evans Contracting into a robot hire and repair business while keeping a cash reserve in case it doesn't take off.
S2.feel: Uneasy, but too busy to dwell on it.
S2.quote: I'd sit Dai down in the cab of his old baler and tell him it's being sold, and I don't know how I'd say it.
S2.fieldNote: Gareth's confidence takes a hit here because his contracting business depends on neighbours not owning the machines. His instant pivot is to robot hire and repair. The moment he dreads is telling Dai his old baler is being sold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a lot of time for anyone who wants to work. I'd say young people should get into robot repair and maintenance now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years suits me. I'd be first again, robot hire, robot repair, before anyone else in the valley. That's my favourite position.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd buy two robots and start hiring them out. By year two I'd set up a repair workshop in the old cattle shed, with my two youngest drivers trained up. I'd let the older tractors go one by one as the work shifts. And I'd put Owen through the college's engineering course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like I know where I'm going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. The big companies might do their own repairs and cut me out. Being first only works if the big boys don't turn up the year after with ten of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about chapel and the community?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to help the young lads in the valley get into the repair work. That's better than any handout. The chapel could host a training evening, why not.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty of time for anyone who wants to work. Young people should get into robot repair and maintenance now.
S3.think: Privately five years suits me, since I'd be first again with robot hire and repair before anyone else in the valley. That's my favourite position.
S3.do: Buys two robots to hire out in the first year and sets up a repair workshop in the old cattle shed by year two, training his youngest drivers. Phases out older tractors as work shifts and puts Owen through the college engineering course.
S3.feel: Calm, as though he knows where he's going.
S3.quote: Being first only works if the big boys don't turn up the year after with ten of everything.
S3.fieldNote: Five years puts Gareth back in his favourite spot, first in the valley. He does see a risk that large companies could cut him out. His idea of community help is training young people for repair work rather than handouts, with the chapel as host.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare can't say they weren't told. I'd say the market will sort out who's ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be 53, with a robot business built up and the farm paid off. Ten years is almost too long, the big firms catch up. I'd still be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build up the robot hire and repair slowly, a robot a year as prices drop. I'd keep the sheep and cattle as the base. I'd keep my drivers on, retraining the ones who want it. And I'd help Owen and Megan into whatever they want, though I'd push for something practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe too calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Too calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I mean, it's easy to say when you're doing well. I'll be honest, I'm more worried the robots come too slowly than too fast. That's not something I'd say at the mart.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Megan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Megan's eleven, she wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to go for it and learn the machines too. There's no harm in knowing both.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, and anyone who doesn't prepare can't say they weren't told. The market will sort out who's ready.
S4.think: Privately I'd be 53 with a robot business built and the farm paid off. Ten years is almost too long, since the big firms catch up, but I'd still be fine.
S4.do: Builds the robot hire and repair business slowly, adding a robot a year as prices fall, and keeps the sheep and cattle as the base. Retrains drivers who want it and helps Owen and Megan into practical careers.
S4.feel: Calm, maybe too calm, as he admits.
S4.quote: I'll be honest, I'm more worried the robots come too slowly than too fast.
S4.fieldNote: Gareth is unusual in worrying that change comes too slowly, which he says he'd never admit at the mart. His free-market line is firm, though he admits it's easy to say when doing well. Ten years removes his early-mover edge, not his security.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the contracting could dry up before I'd turned it round. What would help is the government keeping its hands off and not loading us with rules, and the colleges training young people in robot repair fast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the land. Robots or not, sheep need hills and cattle need grass. Whoever owns the land still matters, and I'd want farming families to keep it.

headlineQuote: I was the first in the valley with GPS, the first with a drone, and I'll be the first with whatever's next, because the first one makes the money.
portrait: Gareth Evans is 43 and runs Pen-y-Bryn, a sheep and beef farm, alongside Evans Contracting, which does silage, baling and spraying for neighbours with five drivers. He uses AI every day and prides himself on being first in the valley with every new machine. He's firmly free-market and wants government out of the way, preferring training and work over handouts. He's calm in almost every scenario, only uneasy with AGI in two years because his contracting could dry up, and he admits he's more worried the robots come too slowly than too fast.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because his contracting business could dry up before he'd turned it into robot hire and repair.
whatWouldHelp: Government keeping out of the way without heavy rules, and colleges training young people in robot repair quickly.
